## Overview

The Cayuse are a Native American tribe in what is now Oregon in the United States. They called themselves *Liksiyu* in the Cayuse language. Their traditional territory included northeastern Oregon and southeastern Washington, from the Blue Mountains to the Deschutes River and along the Umatilla, Grand Ronde, Burnt, Powder, John Day, Snake, Tucannon, Walla Walla, and Touchet rivers. They lived adjacent to the Nez Perce and had close associations with the Walla Walla. Today they share a reservation and government in northeastern Oregon with the Umatilla and Walla Walla as part of the Confederated Tribes of the Umatilla Indian Reservation, near Pendleton at the base of the Blue Mountains. The Cayuse language was an isolate and is extinct.

## Material culture

### Clothing & dress

The sources used describe clothing only in general terms. Women processed animal skins to make materials for clothing, while adults among the Cayuse captives made clothing for the tribe.

### Architecture

The Cayuse were seminomadic and maintained summer and winter villages at sites along rivers in present-day Washington and Oregon. They lived in teepees, which the sources describe as portable dwellings used by nomadic tribes.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

They record horses, dogs, animal skins, salmon, roots, berries, and other materials connected with movement, hunting, fishing, gathering, shelter, and clothing.

## Festivals & rituals

They do describe seasonal movement between summer and winter villages, winter fishing along rivers, annual journeys over the Rocky Mountains to hunt buffalo, and harvesting practices involving salmon, game, berries, wild celery, and roots. The sources also record the Cayuse attack on the Whitman mission in 1847, the subsequent Cayuse War, and the 1855 Treaty of Walla Walla, but do not present these as ritual traditions.

## Foodways

Salmon from the Columbia River was one of the Cayuse’s main food sources. During winter, many Cayuse traditionally gathered in winter villages along rivers to fish for sustenance. They also ate trout and lamprey, hunted elk and deer, and hunted small game such as rabbits and fowl. Women gathered berries, including serviceberries, chokeberries, and currants, and gathered wild celery and camas; they also dug and processed roots. The men hunted and fished, while the women gathered and processed plant foods and animal skins. In some cases, traditional harvesting practices continue to the present day.

## Oral tradition & literature

They record the Cayuse language, historical accounts, village traditions, and named leaders, including Tawatoy, Weatenatemany, Five Crows, and Anna Minthorn Wannassay.

## Language & religion

Cayuse was an extinct language isolate once spoken by the Cayuse people, whose autonym was *Liksiyu*. The first written vocabulary was published by Horatio Hale in 1846. The language was discussed in relation to Molala and the proposed Waiilatpuan and Plateau Penutian classifications, but later analysis questioned the relationship between Cayuse and Molala. The Cayuse language is described as extinct since the 1930s; the sources also state that it was believed to have become extinct by 1902. *Weyíiletpuu* was a dialect of the Nez Perce language spoken by Cayuse inhabitants of the Confederated Tribes of the Umatilla Indian Reservation and has not been used since the 1940s.

## Sources & further reading

- Robert H. Ruby and John A. Brown, *The Cayuse Indians: Imperial Tribesmen Of Old Oregon*. University of Oklahoma Press, 1972.
- Clifford E. Trafzer, *Yakima, Palouse, Cayuse, Umatilla, Walla Walla, and Wanapum Indians*. Scarecrow Press, 1992.
- [Cayuse people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cayuse_people)
- [Cayuse language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cayuse_language)

commons_photos.credit: File URL IIIF manifest Catalog record
commons_photos.description: A Native American women, identified as Eat-no-meat and a member of the Cayuse Tribe, is standing outside in front of a blanket. She is wearing a Euro-American style dress, a necklace, a leather belt, earrings, and a blanket wrapped around her shoulders. Her hair has been tied into braids. She is carrying a bag in her left hand. The name is probably a translation of her Indian name; tribal members are attempting to verify her name.
commons_photos.source_category: Photographs of the Cayuse people by Lee Moorhouse

commons_photos.title: Chief Red Hawk Cayuse Tribe - DPLA - a49f840fb1b89ba393fb98b11adfcab3.jpg
commons_photos.credit: File URL IIIF manifest Catalog record
commons_photos.description: A Native American man, identified as Chief Red Hawk of the Cayuse Tribe, is seated in front of a solid colored blanket that is suspended like a backdrop. The man is wearing a cloth shirt and has a Pendleton blanket wrapped around his body from the chest down. He has long hair, some of which is tied in a scarf that drapes over his shoulder. He is wearing a beaded choker and beaded bracelets. In his lap, one hand is holding a bow and two arrows and a pipe with a long, flat, wooden handle. His other hand is holding up a war club, which is adorned with feathers. A cowboy hat with a braided or twisted scarf hat band is hung on the backdrop. The image appears to be an outside photograph, as there is some vegetation visible in the bottom corners.

commons_photos.title: Chief Ume-Somkin—Cayuse Tribe - DPLA - 8a9c2676c09fd169da119fb6fcc58f51.jpg
commons_photos.credit: File URL IIIF manifest Catalog record
commons_photos.description: An outside photograph of a Native American man who has been identified as Uma-Som-Kin. He is standing with a horse and dog to his left, and a tipi behind him. His hair is in braids with hair ornaments or ties attached to their ends and he is wearing a cowboy hat. He is dressed in a shirt, and over that a coat made out of a Pendleton Blanket. In his right hand he is holding a rifle, and in his left hand both a hand drum and horse reins. He is wearing either calf-high boots or moccasins. The horse or pony has a spotted coat; it is bareback with what appears to be a leather halter. The dog is between the horse and man. It also has a mottled or spotted coat, with uncropped ears and unknown breed heritage. The tipi is made of canvas layers. There is a cloth or canvas doorway directly behind the man; on the back of the tipi leans a broken tule mat. commons_photos.title: Dr. Whirlwind, Cayuse Indian, on horse - DPLA - 75f77e99709c363c47e9b4b4df5fd6bd.jpg
commons_photos.credit: File URL IIIF manifest Catalog record
commons_photos.description: A Native American man, identified as Dr. Whirl-wind (Charley Whirlwind, Sr.) of the Cayuse Tribe, is mounted on a horse. The man is wearing buckskin pants and shirt and moccasins. The shirt is decorated with feathers and beadwork on the front and sleeves. He is wearing a headdress with a full crown of feathers and strips of fur hanging down around his shoulders. He has a large beaded choker. The horse is solid brown in color and has a saddle, saddle blanket and bridle. On the ground in front of the horse is a dog with long, fluffy white hair. The man, horse, and dog are on a slope on the side of a mountain. Around them are some other slopes and some stands of pine trees. The top of the mountain is in the background.
